title: Digital Age ~ CLO6 Launch Event Replay [Continuously Updating] p02 Speech by CLO Founder Jaden
description: Missed the live stream? No time to watch it live? No worries! The recorded video of the CLO6 launch event is here~ Come check it out!
transcript:
Hello everyone, thank you very much to all the guests for taking time out of their busy schedules to attend our Cologne 6 press conference and user exchange conference.  
In fact, during the preparation stage, we were a little worried that because of the epidemic, many users might not be able to come in person.  
But now that we have so many new friends and old friends sitting together, we are very pleased.  
On the one hand, this shows that everyone is very supportive of our work.  
On the other hand, I also feel that everyone needs such a platform to interact and learn from each other.  

This is already our second user exchange conference.  
We hope to continue this event regularly.  
Every year, we provide such a platform to our users,  
so that everyone can interact about some of the pain points and difficulties in the 3D transformation process,  
or share some of the excitement and surprises during usage,  
to help us improve our products better and then provide better services to everyone.  

Today, our schedule is quite tight.  
You may have seen this from the schedule table.  
We also hope to present more content to everyone in a limited time.  

First of all, we would like to invite Jaden Oh, the founder of CLO.  
He will introduce the development process of CLO to everyone through a video.  
After the video finishes, he will connect live from Korea.  
If you have any questions about CLO, you can ask him directly.  

Now, let's first learn about the development process of CLO through this video.  

---

Hello.  
I am Jaden Oh.  
I am the founder of CLO Virtual Fashion.  
It is a pity to talk about this video due to COVID-19,  
but it is really nice to meet the Chinese users for the first time.  

Today, we are going to talk about how our company has grown from a user and technology point of view.  
Our company was founded in 2009.  
And in the video you can see now,  
this is the first version of CLO's software.  
Although it was not widely used,  
it is the first product made with the idea of targeting fashion designers.  
Let's take a look.  

It was a product that was reflected in real-time 3D  
by using fast simulation technology to modify the pattern like this.  
The color and texture were also changed.  
At that time, I believed that this product would be used well in the actual work of a fashion designer.  
However, most of the reactions were,  
“It looks fun, but I can't use it.”  
So, at the fashion school, it was useful for education.  
So, I went to various fashion schools to introduce it.  

Then, for the first time, I really needed our software,  
and I met the person I had been waiting for.  
It's this person.  
His hobby is fun.  
It's virtual cosplay.  
What he does as a hobby is to dress up as a virtual character like this.  

But why was he enthusiastic about our software?  
Why was he enthusiastic about our software?  
I looked at why.  
The existing tools have to make wrinkles one by one like this in 3D.  
If you want to fix something, you have to do it again from the beginning.  
So only CG experts could make clothes.  
And people who do this as a hobby of virtual cosplay  
It was a situation where I couldn't even imagine making clothes.  

For this reason, people who do virtual cosplay as a hobby  
became enthusiastic about our tool.  
I looked at this market.  
There are 2 million users worldwide.  
It is even possible to sell clothes.  
You can make about 1,000 dollars a month.  

So I started adding the features that these users wanted.  
To bring avatars,  
I developed the OBJ Collada File Import function.  
I added various functions and commercialized them.  

That's how it came out.  
This is the Marvelous Designer 2 that came out at the end of 2010.  
If you look at the demo,  
from this point on, you can see that the feeling of commercial software is a little better.  
Avatars, clothes, UI, etc. are much better.  
Also, virtual cosplay users can easily buy software.  
I also built a website that can be sold online.  

As time went by, there was a rumor.  
Suddenly, I got a call from a large CG studio called Weta Digital.  
Because the demand for making clothes for digital characters was the same.  
Not only virtual cosplay users, but also CG companies.  

It began to be used by CG companies.  
At Weta Digital,  
when we made Tintin,  
we started using our software for the first time.  
This costume is the first costume made with our software.  

After years of hard work,  
currently, almost all CG, computer graphics, and studios  
are going to make movies and animations with our software.  
The same goes for Pixar.  

After the movie market, our software has also begun to be used in the computer game market.  
Our software is being used to make clothes in most games.  

How was the fashion industry while there were more users in the film and animation game field?  
CLO has also been released from the beginning with the CG software, but there were no real users.  
It was just a trial of a few companies and a few pattern CAD companies.  

However, we received functional requests from these users and continued to develop.  
The first target was a fashion designer.  
Because we knew that the functionality and usability were insufficient, we added the DXF compatibility function to make pattern companies use it.  
We also added the avatar sizing function, which was the biggest demand at the time.  

However, there were still no users.  
Because there were no users, it was difficult to figure out what the real problem was.  
So we decided.  
We went directly to the actual companies and verified it with our software.  
It was a Proof of Concept (POC).  

At that time, I was interested in Diesel, Steph, Adidas, Louis Vuitton, etc.  
I analyzed the requirements of the POC and continued to develop.  

In the beginning, we developed a lot of functions to improve usability, such as DAW.  
The representative is this internal component cross-interference allowance.  
It's hard to believe, but in the past, the necessary internal component cross-interference was not allowed to make padding, so we had to split the components one by one.  
It must have been really hard.  

There was also a time when there was no 3D undo function.  
We developed various functions to improve usability, including one-to-n sewing, freeze, strengthen, press, tag, m-to-n sewing, etc.  

Meanwhile, we are developing must-have features that fashion users really need:  
stitch, button, piping, measure function,  
sim tape, colorway,  
fabric kit, puckering, rendering, etc.  
All of these are necessary functions.  

Also, as pattern companies started to make patterns in CLO, not CAD, they began to develop various CAD functions for pattern companies in earnest.  
These are the functions.  

And recently, fashion designers have also started to design using CLO.  
I started to install various functions for designers.  

In addition, by installing high-end rendering functions,  
users began to create works like real life.  

After four years of effort, users began to increase in earnest since 2017.  
This year, the number of real-life users has increased by nearly three times compared to last year.  

Currently, many fashion companies are innovating the process using CLO.  
Digital fashion innovation, which started from the field of virtual cosplay, has moved on to the fields of movies, games, and fashion.  

Then, what will happen in the future?  
All users in the fields of movies, games, and fashion were experts.  
We are now trying to create software that can be designed by ordinary people, that is, people who do not know patterns, and your family.  

With this goal in mind, we have recently developed various automation functions.  
Auto-grading allows you to adjust the pattern size according to the avatar size with a single mouse click without pattern knowledge.  

Auto-Sewing is in version 6.0, and if you just place the pattern like in this video, it will be automatically sewn.  
It automatically makes it possible to adjust the size and pose without the help of other people.  
This video is the result.  

Now it's the last one.

Thank you for watching.

Thank you.

chunks.content: # Digital Age ~ CLO6 Launch Event Replay ## Speech by CLO Founder Jaden Oh This document presents a cleaned, structured, and detailed transcript of the CLO6 launch event featuring Jaden Oh, founder of CLO Virtual Fashion. It covers the company’s software development history, technical features, user interaction, and future directions in 3D fashion design, simulation, and virtual apparel production. --- ## Introduction and Purpose of the User Exchange Conference This section outlines the motivation behind hosting the CLO user exchange conferences, emphasizing community interaction, product feedback, and knowledge sharing in 3D digital fashion transformation. - The CLO user exchange conference aims to provide a platform for users to discuss challenges and share insights related to 3D garment transformation. - Despite concerns about attendance due to the COVID-19 pandemic, many new and returning users participated, indicating strong community support. - The conference is intended to be an annual event to foster ongoing communication and product improvement. --- ## CLO Company and Software Development History This section details the evolution of CLO Virtual Fashion from its founding in 2009, highlighting the software’s initial focus, user base growth, and expansion into multiple industries such as film, gaming, and fashion. - CLO Virtual Fashion was founded in 2009 with a focus on creating software tailored for fashion designers. - The first CLO software version offered real-time 3D fast simulation for pattern modification, with color and texture changes, primarily used in fashion education. - Early user adoption was limited due to complexity; however, virtual cosplay enthusiasts found value as CLO simplified garment creation compared to traditional CG tools requiring manual wrinkle creation. - Virtual cosplay users worldwide number approximately 2 million, with some earning around $1,000 monthly selling virtual clothes. - To support this market, features like OBJ and Collada file import were developed and commercialized, culminating in Marvelous Designer 2 (2010) with improved avatars, UI, and garment functionality. - CLO gained recognition when Weta Digital used it to create costumes for the movie *Tintin*, marking the software’s entry into major CG studios. - Presently, CLO software is widely used in film, animation, and game development, including studios like Pixar. - Fashion industry adoption lagged initially, with limited users from pattern CAD companies and a few brands. - CLO responded to fashion industry needs by adding DXF compatibility, avatar sizing, and conducting Proof of Concept (POC) projects with brands like Diesel, Adidas, and Louis Vuitton to refine functionality. - Usability improvements included adding internal component cross-interference allowance, 3D undo functions, and advanced sewing tools (one-to-n sewing, freeze, strengthen, press, tagging, m-to-n sewing). - Core fashion features developed include stitching, buttons, piping, measurement tools, simulation tape, colorways, fabric kits, puckering effects, and high-end rendering. - As pattern companies transitioned from CAD to CLO, more CAD functionalities were integrated. - Since 2017, real-life user adoption of CLO has tripled, with many fashion companies innovating digital workflows using CLO. - CLO’s digital fashion innovation journey started with virtual cosplay and expanded into movies, games, and fashion.

chunks.content: - Usability improvements included adding internal component cross-interference allowance, 3D undo functions, and advanced sewing tools (one-to-n sewing, freeze, strengthen, press, tagging, m-to-n sewing). - Core fashion features developed include stitching, buttons, piping, measurement tools, simulation tape, colorways, fabric kits, puckering effects, and high-end rendering. - As pattern companies transitioned from CAD to CLO, more CAD functionalities were integrated. - Since 2017, real-life user adoption of CLO has tripled, with many fashion companies innovating digital workflows using CLO. - CLO’s digital fashion innovation journey started with virtual cosplay and expanded into movies, games, and fashion. --- ## Future Vision and Automation Features in CLO This section discusses CLO’s strategic focus on democratizing 3D fashion design for non-experts via automation and usability improvements. - CLO aims to enable ordinary users, including those without pattern-making knowledge, to design garments easily. - Recent automation features include: - **Auto-Grading**: Adjusts pattern sizes to fit different avatar sizes with a single click, requiring no pattern expertise. - **Auto-Sewing (version 6.0)**: Automatically sews patterns placed by users, enabling size and pose adjustments without external help. - Upcoming functionality will allow users to modify style lines directly in 3D, facilitating quick silhouette and style changes. - The goal is to continuously enhance software convenience and accessibility for all user levels. --- ## Simulation Mechanics and Variability This section explains the technical reasons behind slight differences in garment simulation results and the design of the simulation algorithms. - CLO’s simulation algorithms run on multiple CPUs, introducing inherent randomness in collision detection between avatars and clothing. - This randomness causes minor variations in the shape after repeated simulations of the same garment. - Despite these variations, fabric physical properties and overall simulation results remain consistent. - This variability mirrors real-life wearing, where clothes do not fit identically every time. - Such stochastic elements are natural and reflect realistic garment behavior. --- ## Layer Management and Multi-Layer Garment Handling This section covers how CLO manages multiple garment layers in 3D simulation and the software’s layer definition capabilities. - CLO supports layer functions that define which garment pieces are on inner or outer layers. - Since version 5.2, layer simulation has been improved to reflect user expectations: - Users can specify layer order (e.g., pockets on the first layer appear on top, other garment layers underneath). - This ensures realistic layering during simulation and prevents unwanted garment penetration. - The layer system supports two main layers: front (outer) and back (inner). - Advanced layer ordering (e.g., distinguishing multiple pocket layers) is currently limited but evolving. - Users are encouraged to consult CLO experts for complex layering issues. --- ## File Formats and Data Interchange This section discusses CLO’s support for file formats and interoperability considerations. - CLO primarily supports BXF and DXF file formats for pattern data exchange. - DXF formats supported include AMA and ASTM variants. - Requests to support additional CAD file formats (e.g., TIP, TPP) are considered feasible but require understanding and prioritization.

CLO primarily supports BXF and DXF file formats for pattern data exchange. - DXF formats supported include AMA and ASTM variants. - Requests to support additional CAD file formats (e.g., TIP, TPP) are considered feasible but require understanding and prioritization. - CLO aims to expand format compatibility to accommodate diverse software ecosystems and user needs. --- ## Differentiation Between Marvelous Designer and CLO This section clarifies the market positioning and functional differences between CLO and Marvelous Designer software. - **Marvelous Designer** focuses on content creation for CG industries such as gaming, emphasizing detailed costume design and visual effects. - **CLO** targets the fashion industry with features geared towards production workflows, pattern making, and garment manufacturing. - Over time, the two products have diverged: - Marvelous Designer includes CG-specific tools. - CLO integrates fashion-focused functions for apparel companies. - Future development may see some cross-pollination of features depending on user demand. --- ## Avatar Rigging and 2D CAD Integration This section addresses improvements in avatar manipulation and integration of 2D pattern design within CLO. - Precise control of avatar joints (fingers, feet, head) is challenging, and improvements are planned for easier pose adjustments. - CLO is enhancing 2D CAD capabilities to allow pattern creation and modification directly within CLO without external CAD software. - Many users already create patterns entirely inside CLO, supported by ongoing addition of pattern editing functions. --- ## Fabric Measurement and Material Analysis This section summarizes CLO’s ongoing efforts to automate fabric property measurement and improve simulation accuracy. - Currently, users manually input fabric properties via the fabric kit, which can lead to inconsistencies. - CLO is developing an automatic fabric analyzer to facilitate easier, more accurate fabric property measurement. - A next-generation fabric kit is expected to launch next year, reducing manual steps. - Accurate fabric moisture measurement is critical for fitting accuracy and simulation realism. - CLO has released a fitting service beta (PLOS fitting) in the UK to collect data and improve fitting precision. --- ## Designer-Focused Tools and Cloth Set Platform This section discusses plans for tools tailored to fashion designers focusing on color, texture, and trims rather than pattern changes. - CLO plans to develop a platform (Cloth Set) allowing designers to modify fabric colors, trims (buttons, zippers), and other surface details without altering patterns or silhouettes. - The material configurator will be the first function, followed by trim adjustments. - Cloth Set currently experiences performance issues in China, which CLO is actively working to resolve with high priority. --- ## Use Cases Beyond Apparel: Bags and Accessories This section explores CLO’s approach to simulating non-garment products such as bags and related challenges.

chunks.content: - CLO plans to develop a platform (Cloth Set) allowing designers to modify fabric colors, trims (buttons, zippers), and other surface details without altering patterns or silhouettes. - The material configurator will be the first function, followed by trim adjustments. - Cloth Set currently experiences performance issues in China, which CLO is actively working to resolve with high priority. --- ## Use Cases Beyond Apparel: Bags and Accessories This section explores CLO’s approach to simulating non-garment products such as bags and related challenges. - CLO includes some support for bag simulation using cube-shaped avatars and predefined bag points. - The bag industry requests more diverse avatar shapes corresponding to varied bag silhouettes beyond basic cubes. - Bags differ from garments as they require simulation of rigid and frozen states, involving repeated hardening and freezing steps. - CLO is open to collaborating with users to develop more comprehensive bag simulation models. --- ## Knot and String Simulation Development This section covers ongoing research into simulating knots and strings realistically within CLO. - Knot tying and behavior (tightening, loosening) are complex problems in 3D garment simulation. - CLO is developing specialized string simulation tools enabling users to tie strings on 3D objects. - This feature is under conceptual development, aiming to automate knot tying order and interaction. --- ## Fitting Accuracy and User Satisfaction This section provides insights into CLO’s fitting accuracy and user feedback regarding simulation fidelity. - Fitting accuracy depends heavily on precise fabric moisture and physical property measurements. - User surveys indicate general satisfaction with current fitting accuracy for their needs. - CLO continues accumulating fitting data via released beta services to enhance simulation precision. - Further improvements are planned as data and measurement technology evolve. --- ## Future Directions in Simplified 3D Fashion Design This section outlines CLO’s vision to simplify 3D garment creation, enabling non-experts to design clothing intuitively. - CLO is developing functions to allow users to modify garment silhouettes and styles directly in 3D by adjusting style lines. - The aim is to enable quick, intuitive design changes without requiring comprehensive pattern knowledge. - This democratization of design supports a broad user base, including hobbyists and family members. - Future tools may allow drawing garment outlines on avatars for automatic pattern generation. --- ## Handling Garment
